source_snapshot.title: Meta smart glasses in the UAE: When does hands-free recording become a privacy concern?
source_snapshot.text: Dubai: When someone holds up a smartphone to take a photo or video, it is usually obvious. But with a camera built into everyday glasses, it becomes harder to tell whether someone is looking at you or recording you.As Meta's AI-powered smart glasses become more accessible to UAE consumers through etisalat, their growing availability raises questions about how wearable technology could change expectations of privacy in everyday settings, from shopping malls and cafés to workplaces.While the glasses offer the convenience of hands-free photography, video recording and artificial intelligence (AI) assistance, their capabilities also raise questions about consent, the security of recorded information and how existing privacy laws apply to wearable devices.The issue is not simply whether consumers can own smart glasses in the UAE, but whether they understand their responsibilities when using them around others..Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here..When a pair of glasses becomes a recording deviceMeta's smart glasses combine cameras, microphones, speakers and AI capabilities, allowing wearers to capture photographs and videos, translate speech, identify objects and ask questions about their surroundings without reaching for a smartphone.However, the ability to capture information discreetly raises concerns about how the technology could be misused, particularly if recordings are combined with AI-powered facial recognition tools to identify, profile or harass individuals without their knowledge.Internationally, concerns over wearable recording devices have already prompted restrictions in certain settings. According to Reuters, courts in jurisdictions including Australia, England and New York have introduced restrictions on smart glasses to prevent unauthorised recordings and protect the integrity of legal proceedings.In September 2026, Meta also introduced Ray-Ban Meta Audio, a camera-free version of its smart glasses that retains audio capabilities without allowing users to capture photographs or videos, following months of scrutiny over the privacy implications of its camera-equipped eyewear..The privacy risks that extend beyond the cameraBeyond the immediate concerns surrounding filming in public, cybersecurity experts warn that users should also consider what happens to the information once it has been captured.Maher Yamout, lead security researcher at Kaspersky, explained that AI-powered smart glasses introduce a new set of cybersecurity and privacy risks by combining cameras, microphones, internet connectivity and AI capabilities in a single wearable device.Unlike smartphones, which are typically used consciously and visibly, smart glasses can capture images, conversations and sensitive information in everyday situations without those around the wearer necessarily being aware.“One key concern is the potential exposure of recordings and personal data. If an account linked to the glasses is compromised, or the device is connected to an unsecured network, cybercriminals could potentially gain access to sensitive information, including stored photos, videos, voice recordings and associated account data. Weak passwords, reused credentials and insufficient account protection can further increase this risk,” Yamout said.The risks also extend beyond the device itself to how AI features process and interpret information..One key concern is the potential exposure of recordings and personal data. If an account linked to the glasses is compromised, or the device is connected to an unsecured network, cybercriminals could potentially gain access to sensitive information, including stored photos, videos, voice recordings and associated account data. Weak passwords, reused credentials and insufficient account protection can further increase this risk.Maher Yamout, Lead Security Researcher at Kaspersky.“For example, features that analyse surroundings, identify objects, transcribe conversations or potentially recognise faces could be misused to profile individuals, identify strangers, gather information about their routines or facilitate targeted scams.”Among the concerns highlighted by Yamout was Meta's proposed NameTag facial recognition feature. References to the unreleased feature were discovered in the Meta AI companion application's code in June 2026 and subsequently removed following privacy scrutiny.“Another concern is the possibility of cybercriminals exploiting vulnerabilities in the glasses' software, Bluetooth connectivity or companion mobile applications to intercept data or gain unauthorised access. Users shouldn't assume that because the glasses are a consumer product, their recordings and interactions are automatically secure,” he added..Does being in a public place mean consenting to being filmed?Being in a public space does not automatically mean an individual has consented to being recorded. According to UAE's Cybercrime Law, it expressly extends to photographs taken in public places, meaning that recording someone in a shopping mall, café or other public setting could give rise to legal liability, depending on the circumstances, according to Samuel Moore, senior paralegal at BSA LawNor does a recording necessarily have to be published online for an offence to occur.“Similarly, footage does not need to be shared online for a privacy violation to occur. The law covers the act of recording and retaining electronic images, provided the relevant elements of the offence are established. Even where footage remains on a user's device and is never shared publicly, there may still be a breach of the law,” Moore said..For smart glasses users in the UAE, the convenience of hands-free recording does not override existing privacy protections. Moore explained that while UAE legislation does not specifically address smart glasses, existing laws are broad enough to cover such devices.Under Article 44 of Federal Decree-Law No. 34 of 2021 on Combatting Rumours and Cybercrimes, using information technology for the purpose of breaching another individual's privacy without consent is a criminal offence..According to Moore, individuals convicted of breaching another person's privacy under Article 44 of the Cybercrime Law could face imprisonment of at least six months and/or fines ranging from Dh150,000 to Dh500,000.Where photographs or recordings are electronically altered for the purpose of defaming or abusing another individual, the penalties increase to a minimum of one year's imprisonment and/or fines ranging from Dh250,000 to Dh500,000.Article 56 of the Cybercrime Law also provides for the confiscation of devices used to commit an offence and the deletion of relevant data following a conviction. This could potentially include the smart glasses themselves..Balancing technological innovation with the right to privacyProfessor Fehmida Hussain, head of Computer Engineering and Informatics at Middlesex University Dubai, said smart technology is likely to become increasingly common in everyday life, with wearable devices such as smart glasses representing the next step in its evolution.“Manufacturers are building in features such as visible recording lights, privacy-by-default settings and on-device processing. Regulators and industry are shaping standards that can begin to build public trust.”.Innovation and privacy are not in competition. When responsible users and thoughtful design come together, smart glasses can reach their full potential and earn the trust they need to become a more regular and useful tool.Professor Fehmida Hussain, Head of Computer Engineering & Informatics Middlesex University Dubai.Hussain stressed that while manufacturers and regulators have a role in developing safeguards, the responsible and ethical use of smart glasses also depends on the wearer.“Responsible use starts with understanding what your device captures, where that data is stored and who it is shared with. Wearers should review their privacy settings, keep their accounts secure and update their software regularly. Most importantly, they should respect the people around them by asking permission before recording.”Technological innovation and personal privacy, Hussain added, are not in competition..Pakistan: Why has Punjab banned smart glasses?.Meta launches new AI glasses in UAE with prices starting at Dh1,160.Europe calls for action over ‘pervert’ smart glasses.UAE warns AI users to check permissions before granting camera or location access

claims.claim: In the UAE, Meta smart glasses with hands-free photo and video recording functions have become available.
The availability of these glasses raises privacy concerns in public places.
UAE legislation provides for liability for recording without consent, including fines up to 500,000 dirhams and imprisonment.
Experts warn about data leakage risks and the need for responsible use of the device.
The owner must respect the rights of others and comply with security settings.

summary_ru: 🚇 Умные очки Meta в ОАЭ: вопросы конфиденциальности и закона В ОАЭ стали доступны умные очки Meta с функциями записи фото и видео без рук, что вызывает вопросы о приватности в общественных местах. Законодательство ОАЭ предусматривает ответственность за запись без согласия, включая штрафы до 500 тысяч дирхам и тюремное заключение. Эксперты предупреждают о рисках утечки данных и необходимости ответственного использования устройства. Владелец должен уважать права окружающих и соблюдать настройки безопасности.
